items.title: Hermes Desktop: backend not reliably drained/killed on app quit (stray hermes serve orphans)
items.body:
## Bug

Hermes Desktop's \`before-quit\` handler calls \`stopBackendChild()\` / \`stopAllPoolBackends()\` but doesn't wait for the SIGTERM to actually take effect before letting Electron proceed with quit. If the backend needs longer than expected to exit, the child is orphaned instead of exiting cleanly.

## Fix

In \`apps/desktop/electron/main.ts\`'s \`before-quit\` handler:
- Capture the primary + pooled backend child processes *before* calling \`stopAllPoolBackends()\` (it deletes pool map entries before killing, so reading the pool after yields nothing).
- \`event.preventDefault()\`, hide windows immediately (Cmd-Q should feel instant even though we're delaying the actual process exit), then \`Promise.allSettled\` a bounded wait (5s) for every still-alive child to exit before calling \`app.quit()\`.
- Guard with a one-shot latch so the \`app.quit()\` this schedules doesn't re-enter \`before-quit\` and reschedule the same drain.

Companion to timeout_graceful_shutdown on the Python side (see the uvicorn shutdown-hang issue) — that fix bounds *how long* a backend can take to exit; this fix makes the desktop actually *wait* for it instead of racing ahead.

Verified: 912/912 existing Electron tests pass with this change; manual quit test showed only the gateway process surviving (correct) with no stray \`hermes serve\`.

items.title: browser_tool.py: orphaned Chromium daemons accumulate for weeks despite reaper thread (owner_pid check likely too coarse)
items.body:
## Summary

`browser_tool.py` has a background reaper (`_reap_orphaned_browser_sessions`, called periodically by `_browser_cleanup_thread_worker` and also on `atexit`) that is supposed to kill orphaned `agent-browser` daemons and their Chromium process trees when the owning hermes process has died. In practice, on a long-running gateway instance, orphaned Chromium processes accumulated for **up to 16 days** and were never reaped.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.16.0 (2026.6.5), running as `gateway run` inside an LXC container (Ubuntu 24.04, Proxmox)
- Long-lived gateway process, single PID, running continuously since initial start (19+ days uptime at time of investigation), never restarted or crashed
- `browser.inactivity_timeout: 120` (default) in config.yaml

## Evidence

Found on 2026-08-01 via `ps aux | grep chromium`:

- **117 chromium processes** running, spanning **13 distinct orphaned sessions** (distinguishable by unique `--user-data-dir=/tmp/tmpXXXXXXXX` and `--remote-debugging-port=NNNNN` per session)
- Session start dates: Jul 16, Jul 17, Jul 25, Jul 26 (x2), Jul 27, Jul 29 (x2), Jul 30 (x2), Jul 31 (x2) — i.e. orphans from **16 different days**, continuously accumulating rather than being cleaned up
- Each orphaned session was a full Chromium process tree: main browser process, 2x crashpad_handler, gpu-process, 2x utility (network/storage), 3x renderer — consistent with a full `agent-browser` daemon-managed session that was never torn down
- The owning hermes gateway process itself (`/usr/local/lib/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python -m hermes_cli.main gateway run`) was confirmed alive and running the entire time (single PID since Jul 15, no restarts)
- Load average on the 4-core host reached 8.72 as a direct result
- Killing all 117 processes (`pkill -9 -f "usr/lib/chromium"`) was safe — did not affect the running gateway process, and load average began dropping immediately

## Suspected root cause

Reading `_reap_orphaned_browser_sessions()` (tools/browser_tool.py, ~line 1311):

```python
if os.path.isfile(owner_pid_file):
    try:
        owner_pid = int(Path(owner_pid_file).read_text(...).strip())
        owner_alive = _pid_exists(owner_pid)
    except (ValueError, OSError):
        owner_alive = None

if owner_alive is True:
    # Owner is alive — this session belongs to a live hermes process.
    continue
```

The `owner_pid` file appears to record the **hermes gateway process PID**, not a per-session/per-daemon identifier. On a long-running gateway (the normal/intended operating mode — it's supposed to stay up), `owner_pid` is *always* alive, so `owner_alive is True` short-circuits the reaper for every single daemon that process has ever spawned — the reap loop `continue`s before ever reaching the per-session `_active_sessions` tracking fallback (which is only consulted when `owner_alive is None`, i.e. no owner_pid file at all).

In other words: the ownership check is process-granularity, but it needs to be session/daemon-granularity. A daemon whose *specific* browser session has ended (or crashed) but whose *parent hermes process* is still running (normal operation) is never reaped, because "owner is alive" is treated as sufden for "leave this daemon alone" regardless of whether that daemon still corresponds to a live, tracked session.

This would explain why orphans only accumulate on long-lived gateway processes and never get cleaned up — the reaper effectively only fires for daemons whose *entire hermes process* died (crash/SIGKILL/restart), which is a much rarer case than a browser session/daemon dying independently while the gateway keeps running.

## Suggested fix direction

The reap loop's fallback path (checking `_active_sessions` in the current process) should probably run *unconditionally* when `owner_alive is True` too — not just when `owner_alive is None`. I.e.: if the owner process is this same live process, check whether the session is still tracked in `_active_sessions`; if it isn't (session ended/errored but daemon wasn't torn down), still reap it. Only skip reaping when the owner is a *different, live* hermes process (cross-process safety, which is the scenario `owner_pid` was designed for).

Alternatively/additionally: track owner at daemon-launch granularity (e.g. a monotonic per-session token) rather than raw process PID, so "is the specific session still valid" and "is the owning process still alive" are answered independently.

## Workaround in place

Deployed a blunt daily watchdog (`orphaned-chromium-watchdog.sh`) via cron that kills any `chromium` process older than a configurable threshold (default 6h) regardless of the reaper's internal state, as a safety net. This works but doesn't address the underlying gap — happy to share the script if useful as a reference for a test case, but it's not a substitute for fixing the reaper logic.

## Impact

On resource-constrained hosts (4-core LXC container in this case), this leak drove sustained load average to 8.72, and each orphaned session held ~100-170MB RSS per Chromium sub-process (~1GB+ per orphaned session, ~10GB+ total across 13 sessions) — a real and growing resource leak on any long-running gateway deployment that uses the browser tool regularly.

## Summary

After switching the model via the desktop app's model picker, `config.yaml`'s `custom_providers` model entries can get corrupted: string model names are serialized as **per-character mappings** instead of plain strings.

## Example (observed on v0.19.1, Windows 10)

```yaml
custom_providers:
  - name: fennoai-copy
    base_url: https://api.asxs.top/v1
    models:
      gpt-5.5:
        '0': g
        '1': p
        '2': t
        '3': '-'
        '4': '5'
        '5': .
        '6': '6'
        '7': '-'
        '8': l
        '9': u
        '10': n
        '11': a
        name: gpt-5.5
```

The mapping `{'0':'g','1':'p',...}` decodes to the string `gpt-5.6-luna` — i.e. a model-name string that existed in the config at some point got written out as a character-index dict. Both `fennoai` and `fennoai-copy` providers were affected; in one entry the corruption was cross-contaminated between two model entries (`gpt-5.6-sol`'s mapping decodes to `gpt-5.5`, `gpt-5.5`'s mapping decodes to `gpt-5.6-luna`).

## Impact

- Currently **harmless** in practice: Hermes resolves models by the YAML **key** (`gpt-5.5`), and the character mappings are ignored. Model calls work (76 successful calls observed).
- It is structurally broken config, and anything that reads the `name`/mapping fields (e.g. a future version, or tooling that round-trips the config) can misbehave. It also makes the config very hard to read.

## Likely source

The desktop model picker's config write path serializing a string value as a dict (per-character index → char). This matches a write that happens when the user switches models in the desktop app's input-bar model selector.

## Suggested fix

- In the desktop config-write path, ensure model-name strings are written as YAML strings, never expanded into a character mapping.
- Optionally: on config load, detect and repair/ignore non-string dict shapes under `models.*` (warn + treat the key as the model name).

items.body:
## Summary

The Hermes updater's "close all Hermes processes" requirement is a dead end in practice: even with every Hermes process closed (only the updater itself left running), the update can still refuse and demand that all Hermes processes be closed — and in the worst case the updater process itself ends up terminated, leaving the user stuck with a broken update and no way forward.

## Reproduction / experience (Windows 10, v0.19.0 → v0.19.1 era)

1. Launch an update while the desktop app is running.
2. The updater errors: *"Hermes is still running. Close all Hermes windows and try the update again."*
3. User closes the desktop app and every Hermes-related process (verified: only the updater process remains).
4. The updater still reports the same "another update is already running / Hermes is still running" error — a leftover updater PID from an earlier attempt (PID that no longer exists) keeps the update locked.
5. The user eventually kills the updater process too, and there is no automated help — no `doctor`-style diagnostics, no auto-remediation.

Separately, the "another update is already running (PID X)" guard can hold a stale PID: the original update process died, but the lock isn't cleared, so every retry fails instantly for hours until a reboot.

## Suggested improvements (either would fix the experience)

1. **Auto-terminate blockers**: when an update starts, have the updater (or a launcher with sufficient privileges) automatically close Hermes desktop/gateway processes itself, instead of demanding the user do it manually — or at minimum, detect that the blocking processes are gone/stale and proceed.
2. **Stale-lock recovery**: if the recorded "already running" PID no longer exists, treat the lock as stale and take it over instead of erroring forever.
3. **Failure path → diagnostics**: when an update/install fails, offer an automatic `hermes doctor`-style run that explains why (which process is blocking, stale PID, disk space, network to GitHub, etc.) and suggests the concrete fix.

## Environment

- Hermes v0.19.0 → v0.19.1 updater (Windows 10, desktop install)
- Stale-updater lock persisted across retries for hours; only a reboot cleared it

items.title: Expose authenticated channel-to-session discovery for dashboard PTY sidecars
items.body:
## Problem

The dashboard PTY sidecar event channel can be consumed by authenticated clients, but those clients cannot discover which durable Hermes session is currently active on that channel.

At `003af7f85ce2ebe24b38556d735a0d7678a4a8dd`:

- `/api/pty?channel=...` allocates a per-channel active-session file and injects it as `HERMES_TUI_ACTIVE_SESSION_FILE`.
- The TUI updates that file on create/resume/switch, and `/api/pty` uses it to resume the channel after reconnect.
- `/api/events?channel=...` streams dispatcher frames for the same channel, but does not provide an initial binding record or an authenticated query for the channel's current durable `session_id`.

Relevant source:

- [`hermes_cli/web_server.py` channel active-session tracking](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/003af7f85ce2ebe24b38556d735a0d7678a4a8dd/hermes_cli/web_server.py#L14813-L14841)
- [`/api/pty` active-session fallback](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/003af7f85ce2ebe24b38556d735a0d7678a4a8dd/hermes_cli/web_server.py#L15474-L15505)
- [`/api/events` channel subscription](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/003af7f85ce2ebe24b38556d735a0d7678a4a8dd/hermes_cli/web_server.py#L15668-L15709)

Parsing PTY output is not a safe substitute, and guessing from the session database is ambiguous when several profiles or sessions are active.

## Requested contract

Expose the current channel binding through either:

1. an authenticated, read-only endpoint keyed by channel; or
2. a structured control frame delivered first on `/api/events` subscription and whenever the binding changes.

A minimal response/event could contain:

- channel identifier;
- durable `session_id`;
- profile identity when the channel is profile-scoped;
- a monotonic binding generation or revision;
- binding state such as `bound`, `switching`, or `cleared`.

No prompt, message, reasoning, tool content, PTY bytes, paths, credentials, or environment values are needed.

## Lifecycle expectations

- Publish/update the binding after create, resume, and session switch.
- A newly subscribed event client receives the current binding before later session-scoped events, or receives a generation that lets it reject stale frames.
- `fresh=1`, PTY child exit, registry eviction, and channel teardown clear or replace the binding truthfully.
- Authentication and host/origin checks are at least as strict as `/api/pty` and `/api/events`.
- Concurrent reconnects cannot expose an older binding as current after a newer switch.

## Why this helps

This lets external dashboard/desktop consumers correlate sidecar lifecycle events with the same durable session used by Hermes without scraping terminal output or inventing a parallel session authority.

items.body:
## Bug Description

On a local custom-provider setup (vLLM, `-t metamcp` toolset), a single MCP tool call
(`homeassistant__list_entities`, called with no query filter) returns an oversized JSON
result (the model's own reasoning reported "over 900,000 characters... too much to work
with directly"). Auto-compression exhausts its 3 attempts trying to make room, and the turn
fails — but with two *different* observed failure modes for what looks like the same
underlying condition:

1. Sometimes an explicit error: `Context length exceeded: max compression attempts (3) reached.`
2. Sometimes a **silent** `end_reason: agent_close` with no error message at all, mid-reasoning,
   right before the model would have made the next (data-retrieval) tool call.

This looks related to #61932 (protected recent tail defeats compression) and #62605
(token-estimate gap), but reproduced on a **local custom OpenAI-compatible provider** (not
Desktop/openai-codex), with the added inconsistent-failure-mode wrinkle.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.19.0 (2026.7.20), upstream `eb527605`
- Provider: custom, OpenAI-compatible, local vLLM 0.26.0 serving a Qwen3.5-MoE model
  (compressed-tensors quant), `--max-model-len 131072`
- Hermes config `context_length` for this model: `262144` — note: **larger** than the
  server's actual `--max-model-len 131072`. Possible contributing mismatch, not isolated as
  root cause.
- Compression config: `threshold: 0.5, target_ratio: 0.2, protect_last_n: 20, protect_first_n: 3`
- Invocation: `hermes -z "<prompt>" -t metamcp --yolo --cli`

## Reproduction

1. `hermes -z "<question requiring miner energy consumption>" -t metamcp --yolo --cli`
2. Model calls `homeassistant__list_entities` with no arguments → full entity list returned
   (model's own reasoning: "over 900,000 characters... too much to work with directly")
3. Turn fails.

Reproduced 3x across a 50+ minute window (once right after container start, once again
~47 min later) with the identical prompt — ruling out a simple cold-start/warm-up
explanation.

**Run 1** (`tool_call_count: 2`, `end_reason: agent_close`): turn stopped mid-reasoning
after 2 tool calls (`list_entities`, `search_entities`), right before the planned 3rd call
(`get_statistics`). No error surfaced to the CLI at all — just silence, 37s wall time.

**Run 2** (immediate retry, identical prompt): explicit
`Context length exceeded: max compression attempts (3) reached.` after 2m8s.

## Why this looks related but distinct

- Same failure text/mechanism as #61932 (`protect_last_n`-style: the oversized tool-result
  message is recent, so it sits in the protected tail and can't be shrunk) — but #61932 was
  reported+closed for Desktop/openai-codex; this reproduces on the bare local
  custom-provider CLI oneshot (`-z`) path.
- Possibly related to #62605 (token-estimate gap): this session's recorded
  `input_tokens: 69,545` for the failed turn seems inconsistent with the model's own claim
  that the raw tool result alone was ~900,000 characters (roughly 200-300K tokens on its
  own) — Hermes' size accounting for this tool result may be significantly off, though I
  haven't traced `estimate_request_tokens_rough` myself to confirm.
- New wrinkle not covered by either: **two different failure modes for the same trigger**
  -- sometimes a clean error, sometimes a completely silent `agent_close`. The silent case is
  worse for debuggability -- nothing at all reaches the end user, not even a truncated
  response.

## Suggested angle (observation, not a fix)

#43059 fixed the PDF-specific instance of "one oversized tool result kills the turn" by
refusing to read the file as text at all. A more general fix might cap/summarize individual
MCP tool results above some size threshold *before* they enter the protected tail, since
per #61932 compression can't touch protected-tail content anyway. Happy to share a sanitized
session export if useful.

### Problem

All text in Hermes Agent is LTR. For RTL languages (Persian, Arabic, Hebrew, Urdu), this causes:

- Chat messages force RTL text into wrong alignment
- Mixed Persian/English content breaks bidirectional rendering
- Markdown tables, lists, and blockquotes display incorrectly
- Persian/Arabic filenames in file browser are misaligned

### Proposed Solution

1. **Per-message direction** — Auto-detect text direction from content, or let users set it.
2. **Markdown-aware bidirectionality** — RTL flow for prose, always LTR for code blocks/paths.
3. **UI mirroring** — Sidebar, buttons, and panels mirror when RTL is active.
4. **Config option** — `direction: auto | rtl | ltr` in settings.

### Why

RTL is essential, not cosmetic. Persian/Arabic speakers cannot comfortably use the app without it. Chromium/Electron already has CSS `direction` + `unicode-bidi` — implementation is straightforward.

### Environment

- **OS:** Windows 10/11
- **App:** Hermes Agent Desktop

items.body:
## Summary

The desktop app's **Settings → Custom Endpoints** panel is **not profile-scoped**: it always reads and writes the *primary* backend's config, regardless of which profile is active. This makes the panel show endpoints from the wrong profile ("already exists" for an endpoint that is not in the active profile) and silently save edits to the wrong profile's `config.yaml`.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.19.1 (2026.7.30) · upstream 003af7f8 (installed from git, macOS arm64)
- Desktop app (Hermes.app), two profiles: `default` + `mac-mini`
- Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint (LiteLLM at `http://172.17.9.1:4000/v1`)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run the desktop app with the **default** profile active. Add a custom endpoint via **Settings → Providers → Custom Endpoints** (base URL, API key, model). It is saved to the default profile's `config.yaml` under `providers.<id>` and `model.provider` points at it.
2. Switch the desktop app to a **second profile** (e.g. `mac-mini`). Open **Settings → Models**: the provider dropdown is correctly profile-scoped and does **not** show the custom endpoint (good).
3. Open **Settings → Providers → Custom Endpoints** in the same second profile: the panel *does* show the endpoint from the **default** profile ("LiteLLM" already exists), even though the active profile's config has no such entry.

## Expected behavior

The Custom Endpoints panel must be scoped to the **active profile**, matching Settings → Models. In the active profile, it should show only that profile's endpoints; saving/validating/activating/deleting must target the active profile's `config.yaml` (and its `.env` for the key).

## Actual behavior

- The panel shows the **primary** profile's endpoints regardless of the active profile (misleading "already exists" / "configured" state).
- Saving through the panel writes to the **primary** profile's config even when the user believes they are configuring the active profile.

## Root cause

In `apps/desktop/src/hermes.ts`, the five custom-endpoint API helpers do **not** spread `profileScoped()`, unlike neighboring helpers and unlike the model-options helper used by Settings → Models:

- `getCustomEndpoints()` — line 796
- `saveCustomEndpoint()` — line 802
- `validateCustomEndpoint()` — line 810
- `activateCustomEndpoint()` — line 818
- `deleteCustomEndpoint()` — line 825

For contrast, `deleteEnvVar()` / `revealEnvVar()` (lines 832–848) and `getGlobalModelOptions()` (line 1456) all spread `...profileScoped()`, so they correctly target the active profile's backend. Because `request.profile` is what Electron main uses to route the call to the right backend process (each pooled backend has its own `HERMES_HOME`), the missing spread means the custom-endpoints calls always land on the primary backend.

The backend side (`hermes_cli/web_server.py`, `/api/providers/custom-endpoints*`, lines 7226–7336) already supports the `profile` param for other endpoints; the custom-endpoints routes just never receive it.

## Impact

Multi-profile desktop users get a panel that lies about configuration state and writes to the wrong profile. In our case this manifested as: endpoint registered on the default profile, invisible in Settings → Models on the second profile, while the Custom Endpoints panel claimed it "already exists" — leading to confusion about which profile was configured. Only the CLI path (`hermes config set` / `hermes model`) reliably targets the active profile.

## Suggested fix

Add `...profileScoped()` to the five helpers in `apps/desktop/src/hermes.ts` (lines 796–830), consistent with `getGlobalModelOptions()` and the env helpers. Optionally, verify the backend routes honor the `profile` param the same way other `/api/*` routes do.

items.body:
## Summary

`hermes-agent`'s root `package.json` declares an npm floor that **no supported Node release can satisfy out of the box**:

```json
"engines": {
  "node": ">=20.0.0",
  "npm":  ">=12.0.0"
}
```

Node 20 and Node 22 ship npm 10.x — including the Node that Hermes bundles and manages itself (`~/.hermes/node` → v22.22.3 + npm 10.9.8). So on a clean toolchain the npm floor fails **by construction**.

The updater already knows this and repairs it (`→ Upgrading Hermes-managed npm to satisfy >=12.0.0…`), but only *after* letting two workspace installs fail first. The result is that a **fully successful** `hermes update` prints two complete red `npm error code EBADENGINE` blocks and writes two npm debug logs. It reads as a hard failure; it is not one.

This is a sequencing issue, not a broken update. Everything self-heals.

## Not a duplicate of the adjacent reports

- **#75651 §1** is a *transitive dependency's* engine range (`@icons-pack/react-simple-icons`, `<11.10.0 || >=12.0.0`) hit by npm 11.x in the Desktop installer. Different package, different constraint.
- **#25012 / #45374** propose bundling Node 24 to stop EBADENGINE noise. **That would not fix this one:** Node 24 ships npm 11.x, which is still below the declared floor of 12. Measured on the reporting machine — system Node `v24.14.0` ships npm `11.9.0`. Raising the bundled Node alone leaves `engines.npm >= 12.0.0` unsatisfiable.

## Log (verbatim, from a run that ultimately succeeded)

```
→ Updating Node.js dependencies...
npm error code EBADENGINE
npm error engine Unsupported engine
npm error engine Not compatible with your version of node/npm: hermes-agent@1.0.0
npm error notsup Not compatible with your version of node/npm: hermes-agent@1.0.0
npm error notsup Required: {"node":">=20.0.0","npm":">=12.0.0"}
npm error notsup Actual:   {"npm":"10.9.8","node":"v22.22.3"}
npm error A complete log of this run can be found in: ~/.npm/_logs/…-debug-0.log
npm error code EBADENGINE
   … (identical second block for the second workspace) …
→ Upgrading Hermes-managed npm to satisfy >=12.0.0…
  ✓ npm upgraded to 12.0.2
added 209 packages in 8s
added 468 packages in 3s
  ✓ repo root + ui-tui, web workspaces (desktop skipped)
```

Post-upgrade npm runs are clean — I checked all seven `~/.npm/_logs/*-debug-0.log` written after the upgrade: zero `error` lines.

## Repro

On any machine whose active npm is < 12 (i.e. stock Node 20, 22, or 24):

```
hermes update
```

Two EBADENGINE blocks, then automatic recovery. Once the managed npm has been bumped to 12.x the machine stops reproducing, so this is most visible on fresh installs and on any re-provisioning of `~/.hermes/node`.

## Environment

- macOS (Darwin 25.6.0), Apple Silicon
- hermes-agent 0.19.1, `main` @ `fcd5e2cc6`
- Hermes-managed toolchain: Node v22.22.3, npm 10.9.8 → 12.0.2
- System toolchain (shadowed by `~/.local/bin`): Node v24.14.0, npm 11.9.0

## Suggested fix

Either:

1. **Move the npm-floor check ahead of the first `npm install`.** The upgrade routine already exists and works — running it as a pre-flight instead of a recovery step removes the misleading error blocks entirely; or
2. **Lower `engines.npm`** to what the build actually requires (`>=10`?). If npm 12 is a genuine requirement, option 1 is the one to take, since no current Node ships it.

items.title: [Feature]: Add PinchTab as a native Browser Automation provider

labels.name: sweeper:not-planned
labels.description: Sweeper: closed per standing maintainer policy (design direction)

items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

Hermes currently supports six browser backends — Browserbase, Browser Use, Firecrawl, Camofox, local CDP connect, and the agent-browser CLI — but every local option either requires a full Chromium install managed by Hermes itself, or relies on cloud providers that cost credits and introduce latency. There's no lightweight, self-hosted, provider-agnostic option for users who want fast local browser control without cloud API keys or a heavyweight local runtime. 
**[PinchTab](https://pinchtab.com/)** fills this gap: it's a standalone 12MB Go binary that launches Chrome and exposes a plain HTTP API, using accessibility-tree parsing instead of screenshots to keep token usage low. Note for reviewers: the specific "13x cheaper than Playwright" and token-cost figures circulating online trace back to the project's own promotional material, not an independently reproduced benchmark — don't cite that number as verified fact in the issue, cite it as a vendor claim.

### Proposed Solution

Add PinchTab as a new local provider option alongside Camofox, selectable via `hermes setup tools → Browser Automation → PinchTab`, with configuration handled the same way as existing providers:

- Add `PINCHTAB_HOST` / `PINCHTAB_PORT` (or a single `PINCHTAB_URL`) to `~/.hermes/.env`, since PinchTab runs as a local HTTP server rather than requiring a cloud API key. [pinchtab](https://pinchtab.com/)
- Set `browser.local_provider: pinchtab` in `config.yaml`, mirroring how `cloud_provider: browserbase` is currently set for cloud backends. [hermes-agent.nousresearch](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser)
- Map Hermes's existing tool surface (`browser_navigate`, `browser_click`, `browser_type`, `browser_scroll`, `browser_snapshot`, etc.) to PinchTab's REST endpoints (`/navigate`, `/action`, `/find`) via an internal adapter, similar to how CDP is already abstracted for the `/browser connect` flow. [pinchtab](https://pinchtab.com/)
- Preserve PinchTab's stealth features (navigator.webdriver masking, UA spoofing, session/cookie persistence) as opt-in flags, since these overlap with what Camofox already provides for anti-detection. [emelia](https://emelia.io/hub/pinchtab-browser-ia)
- Explicitly document that this is a **local-only** provider (no cloud fallback), so users understand it doesn't replace Browserbase/Firecrawl for scale or geo-distributed scraping.


### Alternatives Considered

Using PinchTab today via `/browser connect` with a raw CDP endpoint does not work, because PinchTab exposes its own REST schema to clients rather than surfacing a CDP websocket externally — so no adapter currently bridges the two protocols. A DIY MCP server wrapping PinchTab's HTTP API was considered, but that pushes integration work onto every individual user instead of solving it once upstream, which defeats the purpose of a "lightweight, zero-config" option.

Medium (few files, < 300 lines)

items.body:
## Description

Gateway `session.resume` exposes `inflight.assistant` as a **single flat string** of mid-turn prose (thinking chatter + tool narration + partial answer). On Desktop, that dump can be written into (or projected as) the **`text` part** of an assistant row that already has structured `reasoning` / `tool-call` parts.

UI result: normal thought + tools look fine, then an extra **plain-text slab** of the same mid-turn thinking appears between tools and the eventual final answer (a "sandwich"). On each switch, the dump often grows, so the slab gets thicker.

This is separate from #57077 (Thought block **fragments** into multiple Thought entries). Here structure is partially kept, but the flat dump pollutes answer text.

## Environment

- Hermes Desktop (packaged, ~0.19.x)
- Turns with multi-step reasoning and tool calls
- Triggered by session switch or window focus resume mid-turn

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start a Desktop turn with several reasoning segments and at least one tool call.
2. While the turn is still running, switch to another session (or blur/focus the window), then return.
3. Inspect the assistant row(s).

## Expected

Structured parts remain the source of truth: reasoning / tool-call / answer text. Gateway inflight text should not re-render the whole mid-turn dump as a second plain body.

## Actual

- Reasoning and tools may still show correctly.
- An additional plain-text block repeats mid-turn thinking (sometimes including tool chatter).
- Repeating the switch can enlarge the plain-text block.

## Root cause (code pointers)

1. `appendLiveSessionProjection` always materializes `inflight.assistant` as a text-only assistant projection (`assistant-stream-${sessionId}` with a single text part), or folds a longer dump into an existing row as text.
2. `preserveStructuralParts` (resume ordinal reconcile) can carry structure onto a text-only projection, then treat "longer text wins" without requiring the candidate to be a **strict extension** of the existing **answer** text. A dump that starts with thinking is longer than `chatMessageText(structured)` (which only joins `text` parts, not reasoning) but is not a pure extension of the answer.
3. Journal `overlayProjectionRow` has the same "longer projection text wins" behavior when overlaying structure onto a text-only inflight snapshot.

Files (approx.):

- `apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-session-actions/utils.ts` — `appendLiveSessionProjection`, `preserveStructuralParts`, `reconcileResumeMessages`
- `apps/desktop/src/lib/inflight-turn-journal.ts` — `overlayProjectionRow`
- `chatMessageText` only aggregates `type === 'text'` parts (so reasoning is invisible to "longer text" comparisons)

## Suggested fix direction

- Define **strict text extension**: only advance structured answer text when `next.trim().startsWith(previous.trim())` and previous is non-empty.
- If the current turn already has `reasoning` / `tool-call` structure, **do not** append a pure-text inflight projection and **do not** replace answer text with the full dump; only update `pending` / adopt stream id as needed.
- Apply the same strict-extension rule in `overlayProjectionRow` when the journal row is structured.
- When reconciling ordinals: structured local assistant + text-only live projection at the same ordinal should still count as the same live turn even if answer text is still empty (so structure is not dropped).
- Regression tests:
  - structured row + non-extending dump → text unchanged, no extra text-only bubble
  - structured row + pure answer extension (`"partial"` → `"partial and more"`) → text advances
  - empty answer text + tools/reasoning + dump → keep structure, do not add dump as text

## Related

- #57077 / #57432 — Thought fragment coalescing (different failure mode)
- Pair with mid-turn live+journal twin insertion (window/session switch duplicates entire progress under new ids)

## Notes

Reproduced on stock Desktop resume projection behavior; not dependent on third-party plugins.

items.body:
---
title: "[Windows] Update retry fails when updater-started gateway holds venv .pyd lock (releaseBackendLock scope gap)"
labels: ["bug", "windows", "updater"]
---

## Summary

On Windows, retrying an update immediately after a successful one fails with `WinError 5 Access denied` when removing `venv\Lib\site-packages\**\*.pyd` (e.g. `aiohttp/_http_parser.cp311-win_amd64.pyd`). Root cause: the updater itself starts a fresh gateway after a successful update, and that gateway is **not registered** in `backendPool` / `backendConnectionState`, so `releaseBackendLock` cannot kill it on the next attempt. It then spawns MCP sidecars that load the venv's `.pyd` files, and `pip`/`uv` cannot replace them.

## Reproduction (observed 2026-08-01/02, Hermes v0.19.1)

1. Click "Update" in Desktop → update succeeds → updater starts gateway PID 47544 (`hermes_cli.main gateway run`).
2. Immediately click "Retry" (or run `hermes update`) → venv preflight reports:
   `another Hermes process is using this installation: PID 46812 python.exe ...\venv\Scripts\python.EXE ...\scripts\hermes-codewhale-mcp-server.py`
3. Process tree shows: `47544 (gateway, venv python) → 50168 (child, WorkBuddy python 3.11 via PATH) → 46812 (codewhale MCP, venv python)`.
4. Killing the *registered* backend processes does NOT kill 47544, because 47544 was spawned by the updater, not by the desktop's pool/primary machinery.

## Root cause

`releaseBackendLock()` in `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts` (line ~2755) collects PIDs only from:

- `backendConnectionState.getProcess()` (primary window backend)
- `backendPool.values()` (pool backends)

It then `forceKillProcessTree()`s those PIDs and polls `isShimLocked(shim)` (only the venv `hermes.exe` shim) until it's writable (line ~2789-2797). Two gaps:

1. **Scope gap**: a gateway started by the updater itself (after a successful update) is in neither collection. On the *next* update attempt it survives, loads `.pyd` files (via its MCP sidecars), and the venv replace fails. The 15s re-collect loop (line 2802-2818) also only re-reads the same two collections.
2. **Liveness check gap**: `isShimLocked()` only checks the `hermes.exe` shim, not whether any site-packages `.pyd` is still memory-mapped. A process that doesn't map the shim but does map `.pyd` files (an MCP server running from the venv python) can keep the venv locked while the shim appears unlocked.

## Suggested fix

1. Broaden PID discovery in `releaseBackendLock()` to include any process whose command line references the Hermes install/venv (e.g. enumerate via `wmic`/PowerShell `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` filtered on the install root path), not just registered backends.
2. Register updater-started gateway processes (or pass their PID through to the next update's teardown) so a retry can kill them.
3. Change the unlock gate to verify that no venv `.pyd` files are still mapped — e.g. attempt to open-with-delete or use `Get-Process -Module` against the install dir — instead of only polling the shim.

## Workaround (user-side, for now)

Close the desktop completely (Alt+F4, which triggers `before-quit` cleanup), then kill any remaining `Hermes.exe` + hermes-agent python processes before running `hermes update` / pip. A script doing exactly this is at `D:\Hermes\fix-hermes-venv.ps1` (kill Hermes.exe first to prevent auto-respawn of the gateway, then python, then pip).

## Environment

- Windows 10, Hermes v0.19.1, installed via git checkout, venv Python 3.11.15
- Desktop app: `apps/desktop/release/win-unpacked/Hermes.exe`

items.title: [Bug] gateway lifecycle guard false-positives on any direct script execution inside the gateway

labels.name: sweeper:cannot-reproduce
labels.description: Sweeper: could not reproduce on current main

items.body:
## Bug Description

The gateway lifecycle guard (`cron/lifecycle_guard.py`, introduced by the 2026-08-01 update) false-positives on **any terminal command that directly executes a script under the gateway process** (`_HERMES_GATEWAY=1`). Even a completely harmless command like `kakei balance` or `healthcheck.sh --status` is blocked with:

```
Blocked: command or referenced script cannot restart or stop the gateway from inside the gateway process.
```

This breaks **every** script execution from inside the gateway: skill-driven CLI calls (kakei, kondate, training), cron scripts, and the self-healing pipeline — not just actual gateway lifecycle commands.

## Root Cause

Two false-positive paths in the referenced-script recursion:

1. **Non-shell files are re-scanned as shell command lines.** `_contains_unsafe_gateway_action` reads any referenced script and recursively scans its *entire text* as if it were shell command lines. A large Python CLI (e.g. 4,800-line `kakei`) contains `/`-bearing string literals (`//` floor division, `BIN_DIR=/...` assignment RHS, `$(dirname ...)` expansion) that get misidentified as "referenced script paths". One of them (`//`, the root directory) then fails the `S_ISREG` check and triggers fail-closed blocking.

2. **Directories are treated as unsafe.** `_read_referenced_script` returns `unsafe=True` for any non-regular file, including directories. A directory cannot be execve'd and cannot be a "referenced script", so a stray `/` token from path #1 kills the whole command.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run Hermes gateway (`_HERMES_GATEWAY=1`).
2. From inside the gateway (Discord/Telegram/any platform session), execute a harmless script via the terminal tool:
   ```bash
   /home/futo4/kakei/bin/kakei balance
   ```
   or any multi-hundred-line script (Python or shell).
3. Observe the terminal tool returns the "Blocked: command or referenced script cannot restart or stop the gateway" error even though the script contains no lifecycle commands.

Also reproducible directly via the guard function:
```python
from cron.lifecycle_guard import contains_gateway_lifecycle_command_or_referenced_script
contains_gateway_lifecycle_command_or_referenced_script("/home/futo4/kakei/bin/kakei balance", cwd="/home/futo4")
# -> True  (should be False)
```

## Expected Behavior

- Harmless script execution from inside the gateway should **not** be blocked.
- Only actual gateway lifecycle commands (`hermes gateway restart|stop`, `systemctl … hermes-gateway`, `launchctl … hermes-gateway`, `pkill … hermes … gateway`) and shell scripts that *contain* such commands should be blocked.

## Actual Behavior

- Any direct script execution that recursively scans a large/non-shell file is blocked with the lifecycle-guard error.
- kakei / kondate / training / pipeline CLIs all fail from inside the gateway.

## Proposed Fix (locally verified)

Three small changes in `cron/lifecycle_guard.py`:

1. **Only recurse into shell scripts.** Add a `_looks_like_shell_script(text, path)` helper (shebang `#!/bin/sh|bash|dash|ksh|zsh` or `.sh/.bash/.zsh/.ksh` suffix) and skip recursion for non-shell content (Python, binaries, data). Lifecycle commands can only exist in shell scripts.

items.body:
**Version:** 0.18.2, macOS, two profiles on one install, one gateway per profile (the documented multi-profile default).

**Setup:** profile A's gateway runs a custom iMessage plugin platform; profile B's gateway runs the Slack adapter. Kanban tasks are created from B's Slack sessions with auto-subscriptions back to the Slack thread.

**Behavior:** `_kanban_notifier_watcher` gates on dispatch ownership ("only the dispatch-owning gateway opens kanban DBs for notifier polling", gateway/kanban_watchers.py). Which gateway owns `.dispatcher.lock` is a restart race. When profile A's gateway (no Slack adapter) wins, every Slack subscription is skipped — but only at DEBUG ("adapter not connected"), so at default log levels notifications and artifact deliveries just stop with nothing in the logs. In our case they were dead for a full day before we read the source.

**Asks (any of):**
- Log the skip at WARNING when a subscription's platform has no adapter in the dispatch-owning gateway (it's a persistent delivery failure, not a transient).
- Or decouple notifier polling from dispatch ownership per platform, so a gateway with the right adapter can serve its own platform's subscriptions.
- Or document the coupling on the kanban page — "the notifier runs only in the dispatch-owning gateway" appears nowhere in the docs today.

**Workaround that fixed it for us:** pin ownership by setting `kanban.dispatch_in_gateway: false` on every gateway that lacks the messaging adapter the subscriptions need.

items.body:
# Bug Report: `package.json` npm engine constraint blocks valid npm 11 + Node 22 installs

## Summary

The root `package.json` declares `"npm": ">=12.0.0"`, but the current stable npm release line is **11.x** (e.g., `npm 11.16.0`) and ships with Node 22. This causes `npm install` to fail with `EBADENGINE` on an otherwise perfectly compatible system, and `hermes update` reports a partial/unclean Node.js dependency refresh.

## Environment

- **OS:** Kali Linux (rolling)
- **Node.js:** v22.22.2
- **npm:** 11.16.0
- **Hermes Agent:** v0.19.1 (commit 3f497e2b, installed via git at `~/.hermes/hermes-agent`)
- **Install method:** `hermes update` / `npm install --force`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Install current Node LTS (v22) with bundled npm 11.
2. Run `hermes update`, or navigate to the Hermes repo and run `npm install` / `npm install --force`.
3. Observe `EBADENGINE` failure.

### Actual error

```text
npm error code EBADENGINE
npm error engine Unsupported engine
npm error engine Not compatible with your version of node/npm: hermes-agent@1.0.0
npm error notsup Required: {"node":">=20.0.0","npm":">=12.0.0"}
npm error notsup Actual:   {"node":"v22.22.2","npm":"11.16.0"}
```

## Expected Behavior

`npm install` should succeed on Node 22 with the npm version that ships alongside it (npm 11.x), or at minimum with `--force`/`--legacy-peer-deps`.

## Actual Behavior

- `npm install` fails outright.
- `npm install --force` still fails because the root `engines` check is enforced.
- `hermes update` reports:
  - `⚠ npm install failed in repo root`
  - `⚠ Node.js dependency refresh did not complete cleanly; the installation may be in a mixed state`
  - `⚠ Web UI npm install failed (hermes web will not be available)`

## Root Cause

`package.json` line 57:

```json
"engines": {
  "node": ">=20.0.0",
  "npm": ">=12.0.0"
}
```

There is no npm 12 release yet; npm 11 is the current major line. The `>=12.0.0` constraint is impossible to satisfy on a stock Node 22 installation.

## Suggested Fix

Relax the `npm` engine constraint to match a realistically supported lower bound, e.g.:

```json
"engines": {
  "node": ">=20.0.0",
  "npm": ">=10.0.0"
}
```

If Hermes specifically requires npm 11+ features, use `"npm": ">=11.0.0"` instead. Avoid `>=12.0.0` until npm 12 actually exists and is the minimum tested version.

## Impact

- Blocks clean `hermes update` on any system using Node 22/npm 11.
- Leaves the TUI/dashboard Web UI in a mixed dependency state after update.
- Forces users to either manually patch `package.json` or downgrade Node/npm, neither of which is desirable.

## Workaround (for affected users)

Edit `~/.hermes/hermes-agent/package.json` and change `"npm": ">=12.0.0"` to `"npm": ">=10.0.0"` (or `>=11.0.0`), then re-run `npm install`.

---

items.title: [Bug]: cronjob action='run' blocks the calling turn synchronously — inactivity watchdog kills the parent agent at 1800s

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
### Bug Description

`cronjob(action="run")` executes the target job **synchronously and in-process** on the calling agent's thread. Because a cron job is itself a full agent run (execute → save → deliver), this routinely takes many minutes. The calling turn emits no tool activity and no progress heartbeat for that entire window, so the gateway's inactivity watchdog concludes the agent is hung and kills the parent turn.

The job usually completes fine — the user just loses the turn that asked for it, along with any work that turn had in progress.

### Root cause

`tools/cronjob_tools.py:802` → `_execute_job_now()` (line 568) → `run_one_job(job)`:

```python
if normalized in {"run", "run_now", "trigger"}:
    exec_result = _execute_job_now(job)
```

```python
# run_one_job records last_run_at/last_status via mark_job_run ...
processed = run_one_job(job)
```

`run_one_job` is the same execute→save→deliver body the scheduler tick uses. Invoked from the tool it runs to completion on the caller's thread, with no timeout of its own and — critically — no callback into the parent agent's activity tracker.

Meanwhile `gateway/run.py` applies an **inactivity**-based watchdog (`HERMES_AGENT_TIMEOUT` / `agent.gateway_timeout`, default 1800s). Its docstring is explicit that the intent is to allow long runs so long as there is activity:

> Use an *inactivity*-based timeout instead of a wall-clock limit: the agent can run for hours if it's actively calling tools / receiving stream tokens, but a hung API call or stuck tool with no activity for the configured duration is caught and killed. (#4815)

A synchronous `cronjob` run is indistinguishable from a stuck tool under that rule — it is genuinely working, but silently.

### Evidence

Four watchdog kills in a single day on one install, all naming the same tool, all landing within ~3 seconds of the 1800s threshold:

```
04:06:49 ERROR Agent idle for 1803s (timeout 1800s) | last_activity=executing tool: cronjob | iteration=18/500  | tool=cronjob
04:18:57 ERROR Agent idle for 1803s (timeout 1800s) | last_activity=executing tool: cronjob | iteration=20/500  | tool=cronjob
04:42:03 ERROR Agent idle for 1804s (timeout 1800s) | last_activity=executing tool: cronjob | iteration=11/500  | tool=cronjob
07:41:21 ERROR Agent idle for 1802s (timeout 1800s) | last_activity=executing tool: cronjob | iteration=188/500 | tool=cronjob
```

Every idle-timeout kill recorded in the current log names `tool=cronjob`; the only other one in the previous log file is a `tool=none` case. So in practice this tool is the dominant source of watchdog kills on this install.

The resulting turns show a distinctive signature — very long wall-clock, almost no model calls. Classifying today's 442 turns: 36 ran over 30 minutes, of which 21 made >10 API calls (legitimate heavy work), but **11 made ≤2 API calls**. Worst cases:

| wall clock | api_calls | response |
|---|---|---|
| 7,945.8s | 2 | 686 chars |
| 7,757.7s | 2 | 771 chars |
| 6,145.1s | 1 | 75 chars |
| 5,735.9s | 2 | 582 chars |

1.7 hours of wall clock for one model call returning 75 characters is not work — it is a turn parked inside a blocking tool.

### Secondary impact

On Telegram these zombie turns keep their session and progress bubble alive for the full window, so they continue consuming the per-chat message/edit budget while doing nothing. On a busy chat that contributes to flood-control pressure (see #76494, where accumulated long-lived sessions were a precondition for the ban).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a cron job whose prompt takes more than 30 minutes of agent time.
2. From a chat turn, call `cronjob(action="run", job_id=...)`.
3. The parent turn is killed at ~1800s with `Agent idle ... tool=cronjob`, while the job itself continues and completes.

### Expected Behavior

Any of these would resolve it; the first is the smallest change:

1. **Heartbeat during the run.** Have `_execute_job_now` tick the caller's activity tracker (the same signal tool progress uses) so the watchdog sees a working tool rather than a silent one.
2. **Run detached and return immediately.** A manual `run` could claim the job, hand it to the scheduler path, and return "started" with the execution id — the user gets delivery through the job's own `deliver` route regardless. This also matches user expectation that triggering a job is not the same as waiting for it.
3. **Bound the synchronous path.** Apply an explicit timeout inside `_execute_job_now` that is strictly below the agent inactivity timeout, so the failure surfaces as a tool error with context instead of killing the whole turn.

Option 2 is arguably the correct long-term shape, but it changes the tool's contract; option 1 fixes the reported failure without behavior change.

### Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.19.1 (2026.7.30), upstream `4a8eeb5d`
- Python 3.11.15, macOS 15 (Darwin 25.5.0)
- `HERMES_AGENT_TIMEOUT` at default 1800s
- Platforms: Telegram (polling mode) + Slack

items.title: Add parent-scoped list, cancel, and steer controls for live async delegations

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

items.body:
## Problem

A parent agent can dispatch background work with `delegate_task` and receives a complete `deleg_...` handle, but it has no model-facing way to enumerate, cancel, or redirect that live delegation afterward.

Operator surfaces such as `/agents` and the TUI can provide visibility or controls, but a user speaking to the parent through Telegram, another gateway, or the CLI cannot simply ask the parent to list, steer, or cancel its own live work through an authorized in-process path.

A terminal command or skill cannot safely bridge this gap: cancellation and steering depend on in-memory callbacks owned by the running Hermes process. Exposing those callbacks without a strict parent authority boundary would create a confused-deputy control surface.

## Proposed contract

Add one deferred model-facing control surface for live asynchronous delegations:

```text
delegate_control(action="list")
delegate_control(action="cancel", id="deleg_...")
delegate_control(action="steer", id="deleg_...", message="...")
```

List, cancel, and steer belong together because they share authority resolution, target semantics, lifecycle races, and delegation-ID handling.

### Authority

- Capture ownership only from trusted runtime provenance at dispatch.
- Define an owner as `(canonical profile namespace, compression-only parent-conversation root)`.
- Preserve authority across genuine context-compression continuations, while rejecting branches, delegate/subagent/tool sessions, siblings, ambiguous ancestry, cycles, and foreign profiles.
- Never accept profile, owner, session, lineage, or cursor values from model arguments as authority.
- Treat a complete native `deleg_<8 lowercase hex>` ID as an actionable handle, not authorization.
- Return the same opaque `not_found` response for malformed, foreign, missing, terminal, and otherwise inaccessible IDs.

### List

- Return only live delegations owned by the current parent.
- Reuse the existing async-delegation registry rather than creating a parallel lifecycle store.
- Paginate explicitly and report `total_live`, `truncated`, and `next_cursor`.
- Allowlist only the complete delegation ID, live status, batch flag, dispatch time, and bounded goal/role previews.
- Exclude prompts, context, results, errors, routes, models, owner/session fields, callbacks, credentials, and delivery internals.
- Never claim, consume, suppress, replay, or duplicate terminal completion delivery.

### Cancel

- Request cooperative interruption; do not imply hard thread termination.
- Serialize cancellation and steering per live delegation.
- Report `pending` while a competing control callback is in flight.
- Report `accepted` only after interruption was successfully requested.
- If a callback may have applied an irreversible partial interruption before raising, report a stable non-retriable `indeterminate` state rather than retrying blindly or claiming success.
- Ensure session shutdown, `/stop`, and stale-lifecycle interruption cannot miss a child temporarily executing a steering callback.

### Steer

- Queue bounded guidance through the existing safe steering seam.
- Enforce both per-message and cumulative per-live-delegation limits at runtime.
- For batches, target only active children and report `accepted` only when at least one child actually accepts while the delegation remains steerable.
- Let lifecycle cancellation supersede an overlapping steer so both operations cannot report acceptance.
- Preserve native completion behavior when guidance arrives too late to be consumed.

### Footprint

This capability requires structured access to live in-process callbacks and cannot be implemented safely through `terminal` plus a skill. To keep the core narrow, register it in the existing `delegation` toolset while keeping it outside `_HERMES_CORE_TOOLS`, allowing normal progressive tool disclosure through `tool_search`.

Parent/orchestrator conversations may receive the capability according to existing delegation-toolset policy. Leaf agents must not inherit parent control authority.

## Related work

- #70899 adds TUI Mission Control visibility and live steering. This proposal is adjacent rather than duplicative: it provides a model-facing, parent-authorized surface usable from Telegram and other agent conversations. Shared accepted steering seams should be reused where practical.
- #76390 is a Telegram-specific, read-only activity-panel proposal. Informational visibility remains separate from authority-bearing lifecycle control.
- Existing `/agents`, subagent interruption, `/stop`, shutdown, and native terminal-result delivery remain intact.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A parent can list only its own live asynchronous delegations and receives complete native delegation IDs.
2. Authority uses trusted canonical profile provenance plus a proven compression-only parent-conversation root.
3. Genuine compression preserves authority; branches, delegate/subagent/tool sessions, siblings, cycles, ambiguous lineage, and foreign profiles do not inherit it.
4. Malformed, foreign, missing, terminal, and inaccessible targets are indistinguishable through the control API.
5. Listing is bounded, allowlisted, and explicitly paginated without exposing sensitive internals.
6. Cancellation and steering are serialized without invoking callbacks under global registry or child-lifecycle locks.
7. Cancellation callback failures cannot trigger blind retries or false success after potentially partial interruption.
8. Session/global lifecycle interruption supersedes overlapping steering and cannot leave an active child orphaned.
9. Steering enforces runtime message and cumulative budgets and targets only active batch children.
10. Terminal completion delivery remains native and independent of listing/control.
11. The tool is deferred in the existing `delegation` toolset, absent from `_HERMES_CORE_TOOLS`, and unavailable to leaf agents.
12. Focused race, authority, pagination, disclosure, lifecycle, and real temporary-`HERMES_HOME` integration tests cover the complete contract.

## Non-goals

- No TUI panel, Telegram-specific command, or transport-specific control implementation.
- No model-facing internal `subagent_id` API.
- No hard thread termination.
- No pause/resume scheduler or global spawn manager.
- No terminal-result retrieval or history API.
- No persistence or restart resurrection of live callbacks.
- No new configuration key, environment variable, dependency, database migration, or parallel delegation registry.

labels.name: sweeper:cannot-reproduce

items.body:
## Bug Description

The gateway lifecycle guard (`cron/lifecycle_guard.py`) false-positives on any terminal command that references an executable by absolute path from inside the gateway process (`_HERMES_GATEWAY=1`), when that file is a large binary.

## Reproduction (Hermes v0.19.1, v2026.7.30, Linux/Oracle Cloud, systemd user gateway)

Any command containing the absolute venv python path is blocked:

```bash
/home/ubuntu/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python --version
```

Returns the "Blocked: command or referenced script cannot restart or stop the gateway from inside the gateway process" error, even though the command is completely harmless.

## Root Cause

`_iter_referenced_shell_scripts` treats any executable token containing `/` as a "referenced script" and reads the file from disk. The venv `python` is a symlink to a ~15 MB ELF binary. `_read_referenced_script` reads it; size exceeds the 1 MB limit → returns `(None, True)` → `unsafe=True` → the whole command is blocked fail-closed.

This is a sibling of the #76448 false positive, triggered here by **oversized binaries (>1MB)** rather than by floor-division literals or directories.

## Expected Behavior

- Executing a large binary by absolute path should not be blocked.
- The guard should skip non-text files (ELF magic-byte check) and treat oversized binaries as non-scripts instead of fail-closed.

## Workaround

Invoke the executable by bare name via PATH:

```bash
python3 --version   # works
/home/ubuntu/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python --version   # blocked
```

## Environment

- Hermes v0.19.1 (v2026.7.30), git install
- Linux (Oracle Cloud, Ubuntu), gateway as systemd user service
- `tools/terminal_tool.py` guard path (`_HERMES_GATEWAY=1`)

items.title: [Bug]: Copilot token exchange stalls startup ~4.5s because `_is_suppressed()` is checked after the exchange

labels.name: comp/agent

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
### Summary

`_is_suppressed()` is checked **after** `get_copilot_api_token()` in the copilot branch of `agent/credential_pool.py`. Because the exchange retries 3× with a 1.5s/3.0s backoff, every startup pays **~4.5 s of pure sleep** on machines where `gh` is authenticated but the user has no Copilot subscription — and `hermes auth remove copilot` cannot stop it, since suppression only prevents the pool entry, not the exchange.

### Environment

- Hermes commit `baec57de66`, version `0.19.1`
- macOS 26 (Apple Silicon), local-only provider (custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint)
- `gh` authenticated with a `gho_*` token (for git/issues), **no Copilot subscription**
- No `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` / `GH_TOKEN` / `GITHUB_TOKEN` set

### Steps to reproduce

1. `gh auth login` (produces a `gho_*` token), without a Copilot subscription
2. Start Hermes Desktop
3. Watch `~/.hermes/logs/agent.log`

### Observed

Adjacent-line deltas in `agent.log`, twice per startup:

```
10:15:13.299  tools.tool_search      tool_search activated (tier 1)
     +4.745 s   <- no log output at all
10:15:18.044  agent.credential_pool  Copilot token exchange degraded to RAW token ...
     +5.279 s
10:15:23.415  agent.credential_pool  Copilot token exchange degraded to RAW token ...
```

The numbers match the retry policy exactly:

```python
# hermes_cli/copilot_auth.py
_EXCHANGE_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3
_EXCHANGE_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS = 1.5   # sleeps ~1.5s, ~3.0s between attempts
sleep_s = _EXCHANGE_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS * (attempt + 1)
```

1.5 s + 3.0 s = 4.5 s of sleep, plus three round-trips (~0.19 s each) ≈ 5.1 s.

This is **not** a network problem — measured from the same machine at the same time:

| endpoint | time |
|---|---|
| `api.github.com/copilot_internal/v2/token` | 0.19 s (401) |
| `api.githubcopilot.com` and 4 sibling hosts | 0.09–0.68 s |
| `gh auth token` | 0.04 s |

### Root cause

`agent/credential_pool.py`, copilot branch:

```python
token, source = resolve_copilot_token()
if token:
    api_token, enterprise_base_url = get_copilot_api_token(token)   # <- 3 retries, ~4.5 s
    ...
    source_name = "gh_cli" if "gh" in source.lower() else f"env:{source}"
    if not _is_suppressed(provider, source_name):                   # <- checked only here
```

`hermes auth remove copilot 1` reports *"Suppressed all copilot token sources (gh_cli + env vars) — they will not be re-seeded"*, but the stall persists, because suppression is consulted after the expensive call. `resolve_copilot_token()` offers no opt-out either — it falls back to `gh auth token` unconditionally.

### Suggested fix

Move the `source_name` computation and the `_is_suppressed()` check above the exchange. The **`qwen-oauth` branch immediately below already uses this order** (resolve → `source_name` → `_is_suppressed()` → work), so this only makes copilot consistent with its neighbour. `api_token` / `enterprise_base_url` are not referenced outside the suppression block, so the move is local.

```python
source_name = "gh_cli" if "gh" in source.lower() else f"env:{source}"
if not _is_suppressed(provider, source_name):
    api_token, enterprise_base_url = get_copilot_api_token(token)
    if api_token == token and not enterprise_base_url:
        logger.warning("Copilot token exchange degraded to RAW token ...")
    active_sources.add(source_name)
    ...
```

Verified locally: the "Copilot token exchange degraded" warnings drop from **6 per startup to 0** (the exchange is skipped entirely once suppressed), and the startup sequence stays at ~1.6 s.

### Related

Same trigger (`gh auth token` fallback with no Copilot subscription) as #25246, but a different defect: that issue is about Copilot being *shown* as available, this one is about startup latency and `hermes auth remove` being unable to prevent it. Also adjacent to #47708 and #35946, which concern classic `ghp_*` PATs.

items.body:
# Bug: Git diff/review preview of files fails with "file does not exist" (ENOENT)

> Issue draft for NousResearch/hermes-agent — `apps/desktop`.
> Verified against source at desktop `electron/main.ts` + `electron/hardening.ts`.
> Affected surface: **Project mode → review/diff panel → click a file to preview**.

---

## Summary

When Hermes Desktop is in **Project mode** and the user previews a changed file
from the **git diff / review panel** (the file tree showing `+N / -N` diff
stats), the preview fails with:

```
预览不可用
Error invoking remote method 'hermes:readFileText':
Error: Text preview failed: file does not exist.
```

The same file opens correctly from the **Files browser** (left sidebar). The
file on disk is perfectly fine — this is a **path-resolution bug**, not a
corrupt file.

## Environment

- Hermes Desktop (Electron), local profile, Project mode
- Repo path contains a space: `/home/lexyao/Memory Star Map`
- File e.g. `projects/pending/ai-agent-ranking/status.md` (exists, valid markdown)

## Reproduction

1. Open any git repo in **Project mode**.
2. Open the **review / diff** panel (the file tree with `+N / -N` columns).
3. Click a changed `*.md` (or any text) file to preview it.
4. Observe: `预览不可用` + `hermes:readFileText ... file does not exist`.
5. Open the **same file** from the **Files** sidebar → preview works.

## Root cause

The renderer invokes `readFileText(file)` with a **repo-relative path**
(e.g. `projects/pending/ai-agent-ranking/status.md`) coming from the git diff
blob, but the IPC handler resolves it against `process.cwd()` instead of the
repo root.

`electron/main.ts:10376`

```ts
ipcMain.handle('hermes:readFileText', async (_event, filePath) => {
  const { resolvedPath, stat } = await resolveReadableFileForIpc(filePath, {
    purpose: 'File preview',
  })
  //                                              ^^^ no baseDir passed
  ...
})
```

`electron/hardening.ts:206-213` — when `baseDir` is omitted, resolution falls
back to `process.cwd()`:

```ts
const baseInput = typeof options.baseDir === 'string' && options.baseDir.trim()
  ? options.baseDir
  : process.cwd()
const resolvedBase = path.resolve(safeBaseInput)
const resolvedPath = path.resolve(resolvedBase, raw)   // <-- raw is repo-relative
rejectUnsafePathSyntax(resolvedPath, purpose)
return resolvedPath
```

`electron/hardening.ts:222-223` — the wrong path then fails `stat` with `ENOENT`
and surfaces as "file does not exist":

```ts
if (code === 'ENOENT' || code === 'ENOTDIR') {
  throw ipcPathError(code || 'ENOENT', `${purpose} failed: ${typeLabel} does not exist.`)
}
```

The **space in the repo path is NOT the cause** — `path.resolve` handles spaces
correctly; the failure is purely that a repo-relative path is joined onto the
wrong base directory.

The diff-preview entry point lives in the renderer (see
`apps/desktop/src/lib/local-preview.ts` and
`apps/desktop/src/contrib/runtime-loader.ts` calling `desktop.readFileText(file)`);
that call site does not supply the repo root it already knows from the git API.

## Suggested fix

Either:

1. When previewing from the diff/review panel, pass the **git repo root** as
   `baseDir` to `readFileText` (the renderer already obtains the repo root via
   the git API / `gitRoot()` in `desktop-fs.ts`), or
2. In `desktop-fs.ts` `readFileText`, for the `'File preview'` purpose,
   auto-resolve the git root of the input when the path is relative.

Passing `baseDir: <repoRoot>` to `resolveReadableFileForIpc` makes
`path.resolve(resolvedBase, raw)` produce the correct absolute path, matching
what the Files-browser path already does.

## Workaround (until fixed)

Open the file from the **Files** sidebar instead of the diff/review panel.

## Bug Description

A git-installed Hermes Agent v0.19.0 installation on Ubuntu 24 can become stuck in a mixed update state. The updater fast-forwards the Python/source checkout, but the same update run then attempts the Node dependency refresh with an incompatible system npm, reports a warning, and does not automatically retry using Hermes' managed Node runtime.

The user-visible result was that Hermes remained effectively stuck at v0.19.0 from the Desktop user's perspective and the expected Kanban surface was not visible.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start with a git-installed Hermes Agent v0.19.0 on Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64.
2. Have the system runtime at Node v20.20.2 / npm v10.8.2.
3. Run:

   ```bash
   hermes update --backup --yes
   ```

4. Observe that the source checkout advances to v0.19.1, but the Node dependency refresh reports npm engine failures for the repository/workspaces.
5. Relaunch Desktop and check the available UI features.

## Expected Behavior

- The updater should select or provision a compatible Hermes-managed Node/npm runtime before running workspace installs.
- A dependency-refresh failure should either be repaired automatically or cause the update to exit non-zero with a clear retry command.
- Desktop packaging should not proceed as if the installation were healthy when dependency refresh is incomplete.
- Bundled Desktop plugins such as Kanban should have an obvious enablement path or be surfaced clearly in the UI.

## Actual Behavior

The update produced an npm engine mismatch similar to:

```text
npm error code EBADENGINE
Required: npm >= 11.17.0
Actual:   npm 10.8.2
```

The updater reported that the Node dependency refresh did not complete cleanly and that the installation might be in a mixed state. The Desktop package could still be rebuilt using the existing `node_modules`, which masked the incomplete dependency refresh.

After the source update, Kanban code was present in the Desktop package but the plugin was configured with `defaultEnabled: false`. It was not visible until it was manually enabled under **Settings → Plugins**. This made the feature appear to be missing after the update.

## Environment

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64
- Hermes: v0.19.0 upgraded to v0.19.1
- Install method: git checkout
- System Node: v20.20.2
- System npm: v10.8.2
- Hermes-managed runtime available: Node v22.23.2 / npm v12.0.2

## Workaround

Prepending the Hermes-managed runtime and rerunning the workspace installs repaired the installation:

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.hermes/node/bin:$PATH"
cd "$HOME/.hermes/hermes-agent"
npm install --workspaces=false --no-audit --no-fund
npm install --workspace ui-tui --no-audit --no-fund
npm install --workspace web --no-audit --no-fund
cd apps/desktop
npm run pack
```

Kanban then had to be enabled from **Settings → Plugins**.

## Additional Context

This appears related to, but distinct from:

- #75670 — node_modules integrity is not verified after update
- #76486 — npm engine constraint blocks Node 22/npm 11 installs
- #44580 — updater reports success when Desktop rebuild fails

The main issue here is the upgrade handoff for an existing v0.19.0 installation: the updater updates the source first, then leaves dependency repair to an incompatible runtime without a reliable self-healing retry or a hard failure state.
